prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints tie credit to asset prices, so that small shocks are amplified and propagated into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single part for B011, credited to Kiyotaki and Moore. After reading the full round 1 exchange, my reasons have become narrower and more specific. The 1997 paper states one mechanism precisely. Borrowing limits depend on collateral values, and collateral values depend on the borrowing the limits allow. That loop turns small, temporary shocks into large and persistent fluctuations. It is the kind of contribution I value as a mechanism designer, since it has explicit assumptions, a sharp result and a structure that later work could build on and did build on. It is nearly thirty years old, so debate about its validity has had time to settle. The two-author origin makes the credit line short and easy to defend. I read the exchange as showing that the live questions are the 2022 overlap, indirect identification and the Gertler/Gilchrist boundary. None of these seems to me to defeat the achievement, and all of them can be addressed in the citation wording. The chair asked for wording, so I propose the citation above. It names only the collateral-price feedback and does not claim the financial-accelerator strand, bank runs or bank-focused crisis research, or the empirical measurement of the channel's size. Support counts in the opening are not evidence of merit, and I do not rely on them. What persuades me is that the attribution is clean, the idea is mature, and the citation can be worded so that it honours only what Kiyotaki and Moore did.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still the 2022 overlap. The committee may judge that financial frictions and crises are already honoured, even though I read the collateral-price mechanism as distinct from the banking and bank-run analysis. The second reservation is identification. The collateral channel is established mainly as a modelling building block and through indirect crisis evidence, not as a directly measured magnitude. That is a real difference from B005, whose selection and reallocation margins can be checked against firm-level data in many countries. The third is completeness. A two-name award leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose quantitative work carried financial frictions into policy models. Hjalmarsson and Strömberg say they would not object to a broader award, and I cannot say that the narrow reading is the only defensible one. Finally, B005 has the broadest support across all eleven opening rankings. If the committee concludes that the 2022 overlap is decisive, B005 is the stronger fallback. I do not regard the B011 versus B005 choice as lopsided on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B005 and ranks B011 below it. The reasons given are that the 2022 overlap weighs more heavily, and that a credit-cycle model that is conceptually foundational but weakly identified is a different kind of achievement from one with a long record of firm-level testing.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between a foundational mechanism and a directly tested one, and I do not think it can be argued away. Where I differ is on how much it should count. The Nobel tradition has often recognised theoretical mechanisms whose importance shows in how widely they are reused and extended, and B011 has that record. The honest limit is that the citation should credit the mechanism and make no claim about a measured effect size, and I have worded it that way. On the 2022 overlap, I find the distinction between bank runs and information frictions in banking and collateral-driven amplification in the real economy credible, though I cannot verify it independently here. If it persuades you less than it persuades me, that is a legitimate difference in judgement and not a factual dispute. It is also the main reason I keep B005 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B005 and offers three arguments: direct confirmation on firm-level data across many countries, a Helpman-Melitz credit anchored on the heterogeneous-firm extensions and not on the monopolistic-competition base covered in 2008, and a wording that claims the theoretical integration and not the empirical discovery of exporter heterogeneity.
responses.response: That wording would answer much of the attribution objection I raised in round 1, and it moves me. If the committee turned to B005, I could support a citation anchored on selection and reallocation across firms in that form. Two issues remain for me. First, Helpman's marginal credit still depends on the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple export-versus-FDI work and on a boundary with the separate B020 entry, and those lines are harder to draw than the Kiyotaki-Moore line. Second, Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the credited names. Wording can manage that, but it cannot remove it. On the chair's question about a Melitz-centred single credit, I think it is cleaner on attribution but understates what the pairing gives. If the committee did choose B005, I would support the Helpman-Melitz pair over a single name, and I would still leave Redding out.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B005 for its more direct firm-level evidence. He engaged with my two-name argument and says the choice is closer than his opening ranks suggested. He would not add Gertler and Gilchrist to B011 and would not oppose B011 if attribution is handled with the same care.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour, and I read the difference between us in the same way: it is a judgement about which kind of evidence to weight, not a dispute about quality. You also shared my view that a third name would weaken B011, which fits the round 1 convergence on Kiyotaki and Moore alone. I take your point that a committee which weights direct empirical confirmation will put B005 first, and I think that is a respectable position. My answer is that the maturity of B011 and its role as a building block in later work are also forms of confirmation, although more indirect. For the chair's question on which issues are decisive against B005, I would say none is decisive in isolation. Taken together, though, the Krugman overlap, the uncredited contributors and the B020 boundary make the citation harder to draw than for B011.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B012 but says Hassler's argument moved him on B011. He accepts that the 2022 overlap is weaker than he first judged, that a general-equilibrium mechanism through asset prices and credit limits differs from bank runs, and that B011 has cleaner attribution than B012.
responses.response: I welcome that, and I want to be careful not to treat it as support for B011's merit, since you keep B012 first for your own reasons. If your preferred part cannot carry, the chair asked which listed alternative you would support. B011 and B005 are both on your list, and I think the committee would benefit from knowing which you would choose. For my part I share your concern about dispersion in B012. Persson and Tabellini are the core of the rules-and-policy programme, but the literature has many contributors, and the identification weakness you concede is real. I rank B012 below B011 and B005 for that reason. That is not a claim that political economics lacks merit. It is a view that the credit in this particular entry is harder to isolate. I also want to say that your point about citation wording applies equally to B011: the wording must carry the limit on what has been shown.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as having already covered the ground, which would lower the marginal case for B011. My own judgement that the collateral mechanism is distinct rests on general knowledge and has not been independently verified.

Whether the Gertler/Gilchrist accelerator strand should be excluded or credited. I think a two-name award is easier to defend on attribution, but I recognise that it leaves out the strand that brought financial frictions into quantitative policy models, and I would not block a different committee view.

How much weight to place on indirect identification of the collateral channel against the more direct firm-level testing of B005. This is the disagreement I find hardest to resolve, because it is a question about evidence standards and not about facts.

Whether a two-part configuration is possible. Under the three-person cap, B011 plus a one-name B048 part (Rubinstein alone) would technically fit, but it would split the B048 credit away from Wolinsky, rest on thin support in the opening rankings, and add little to a clean B011 award. I therefore propose a single part and do not claim a coherent pairing.
B048 (alternating-offers bargaining) is my second alternative because of my own opening rank. I recognise that only three members ranked it, so it is unlikely to carry as a fallback.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It lists no co-authorship, institutional or other connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, Helpman, Melitz, Redding, Rubinstein, Wolinsky or Binmore, the names in my preferred part and alternatives. My long-time co-authors (Svensson, Ehlers, Erlanson, Martinello, Teytelboym, Trapp, Biró) are not credited on those entries. I am an affiliated professor at the Stockholm School of Economics alongside committee colleagues Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. That is a collegial tie and not a tie to a candidate, and I note that Dreber Almenberg and Strömberg hold different first choices from Friberg. My field is microeconomic theory and market design, so a clean mechanism result may appeal to me more than it should, and B048 is adjacent to my field. My 2020 presentation speech was delivered on behalf of the Academy and does not establish a preference in this simulation. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
